topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: The presence of many different types of people, views, cultures, or identities within a community or society

examples.en-GB: Religious diversity in modern Britain means churches, mosques, synagogues, mandirs, and gurdwaras all exist in the same cities.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: A society in which many different religious and non-religious worldviews coexist and are respected equally

examples.en-GB: Religious pluralism means you do not have to agree with all beliefs to respect those who hold them.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: Relating to non-religious matters; a secular state is neutral on religion rather than favouring or opposing any particular faith

examples.en-GB: A secular school teaches about religions objectively rather than promoting one faith above others.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: The view that religion should be kept separate from public and political life, and that the state should not favour any religion

examples.en-GB: Secularists argue that faith schools are incompatible with a neutral state education system.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: A comprehensive way of understanding the world — including beliefs about meaning, value, purpose, and how to live — whether religious or non-religious

examples.en-GB: Humanism and Christianity are both worldviews, though one is non-religious and one is religious.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Non-Religious Worldviews

data.targetWord: A person who does not believe in God or gods

examples.en-GB: An atheist bases their ethics on reason and human experience rather than religious teaching.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Non-Religious Worldviews

data.targetWord: A person who holds that whether God exists is unknown or unknowable — neither affirming nor denying God's existence

examples.en-GB: An agnostic is not certain whether God exists and may feel the question cannot be definitively answered.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Non-Religious Worldviews

data.targetWord: A person who bases their values and ethics on human reason, empathy, and concern for wellbeing rather than on religious belief

examples.en-GB: Humanists hold ceremonies for weddings and funerals that celebrate human life without reference to God.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Data and Society

data.targetWord: An official survey of the entire population, conducted every ten years in the UK, including questions about religious identity

examples.en-GB: The 2021 census showed that less than half the population of England and Wales identified as Christian.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Community

data.targetWord: Involving two or more different religious traditions working together, in dialogue, or cooperating on shared concerns

examples.en-GB: Interfaith forums bring religious leaders together to discuss community issues and build mutual understanding.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Community

data.targetWord: The building of strong, positive, and trusting relationships between different groups in society — including those of different faiths, ethnicities, and backgrounds

examples.en-GB: Community cohesion events bring different religious and cultural groups together for shared activities.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Identity

data.targetWord: A person's sense of who they are — which may include religion, ethnicity, nationality, family, culture, and personal values, often overlapping in complex ways

examples.en-GB: A person's religious identity may be just one part of a broader identity that also includes nationality, language, and culture.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Law and Rights

data.targetWord: A quality that the law protects from discrimination — religion or belief is one of the nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010

examples.en-GB: Religion or belief is a protected characteristic, meaning employers cannot refuse to hire someone because of their faith.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Public Life

data.targetWord: Religious and pastoral support offered in hospitals, schools, prisons, and the military by chaplains who support people of all faiths and none

examples.en-GB: Hospital chaplains provide spiritual support to patients of all faiths and non-religious patients too.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Identity

data.targetWord: Containing and valuing many cultures; a multicultural society recognises diverse cultural traditions as part of its identity

examples.en-GB: Britain is a multicultural society where people from many countries, cultures, and faiths contribute to national life.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: Treating someone unfairly or less favourably because of who they are — including their religion, ethnicity, gender, or other characteristic

examples.en-GB: Refusing to employ someone because of their religion is unlawful discrimination in the UK.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Challenges

data.targetWord: Prejudice, hostility, or discrimination directed against Muslims or Islam — including hate crimes, stereotyping, and the portrayal of all Muslims as dangerous

examples.en-GB: Islamophobia includes assuming all Muslims hold extremist views, which is a harmful stereotype.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Challenges

data.targetWord: Prejudice, hostility, or hatred directed against Jewish people — one of the oldest forms of religious hatred, which has increased in recent years in Britain and Europe

examples.en-GB: Antisemitism includes conspiracy theories, Holocaust denial, and attacks on Jewish individuals or synagogues.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Key Concepts

data.targetWord: An unfair, negative opinion about a person or group formed without evidence or genuine knowledge — often based on fear or stereotypes

examples.en-GB: Assuming all religious people are intolerant is prejudice that ignores the diversity of religious belief and practice.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Public Life

data.targetWord: A church that is officially recognised as the state church of a country — in England, this is the Church of England, whose monarch is also head of state

examples.en-GB: As the established church, the Church of England has bishops who sit in the House of Lords.

Communities work alongside each other, building trust through shared action

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Media Literacy

data.title: Put these steps of critically analysing a media report about a religious community in the correct order.
items: Read the headline and notice what religion (if any) is named
Ask: would a similar story about a different group name that group's religion?
Identify whether the report describes one person's action or implies something about the whole community
Consider: is there evidence to support the implicit claim, or is this a stereotype?
Form a balanced judgement about whether the report is fair and accurate
